extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; scientists and graduate students interested in the conceptual foundations and development of science
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of paradigms, normal science, and scientific revolutions: how communities form standards, how revolutions arise from anomalies, and how paradigms shape research practice and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific revolution (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary episodes that begin when the profession can no longer evade anomalies that subvert the existing tradition of scientific practice; tradition-shattering complements to the tradition-bound activity of normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolutions occur when repeated anomalies cannot be aligned with professional expectation despite effort; they initiate extraordinary investigations and lead the profession to a new set of commitments and a new basis for scientific practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research firmly based upon one or more past scientific achievements that a particular scientific community acknowledges for a time as supplying the foundation for its further practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science proceeds from accepted theory (as recounted in textbooks) and is characterized by commitments to the same rules and standards; it narrows the field of legitimate problems and methods and enables practitioners to concentrate on specific, often esoteric, problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete scientific achievements—examples of actual practice including law, theory, application, and instrumentation—which provide models from which spring coherent traditions of scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paradigm must be sufficiently unprecedented to attract adherents and sufficiently open-ended to leave problems for future practitioners; paradigms define legitimate problems and methods and prepare students for membership in the scientific community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms as prior units for study
rubrics_metrics.description: The concrete scientific achievement (paradigm) is prior to the abstract concepts, laws, and points of view abstracted from it and functions as a fundamental unit for students of scientific development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians should study paradigms (including specialized ones) because they determine what practitioners take for granted and thus shape the subsequent practice of research; answers about why paradigms are fundamental are developed later in the text but depend on exposure to paradigmatic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Anomalies—observations or problems that cannot be reconciled with the existing paradigm—are crucial triggers for extraordinary investigations and the eventual onset of scientific revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science is expected to resolve puzzles within the paradigm; persistent anomalies that resist alignment with professional expectations prompt extraordinary research and competition between traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary replacement (characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions involve the community’s rejection of one time-honored scientific theory in favor of another incompatible one, producing a shift in available problems and in the standards for admissible problems and legitimate problem-solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each revolution transforms the scientific imagination and the world within which work is done; controversies typically accompany such shifts; the process requires reconstruction of prior theory and reevaluation of prior facts and is rarely instantaneous or accomplished by a single person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact and theory inseparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific fact and theory are not categorically separable; discoveries (e.g., oxygen, X‑rays) do more than add items to the scientist's world—they require reevaluation of experimental procedures and conception of entities through the network of theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected discoveries can qualitatively transform the scientist's world as well as quantitatively enrich it; thus discovery can be revolutionary because it alters the conceptual and methodological framework, not merely the inventory of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for paradigm acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: To be accepted as a paradigm, a theory must seem better than its competitors though it need not, and never does, explain all the facts confronting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms are accepted because they provide superior explanatory and problem-directing power (e.g., Franklin's theory accounting for many electrical effects), suggesting which experiments are worth performing and which are secondary; acceptance often ends interschool debate and encourages more precise, esoteric work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Route to a firm research consensus (pre-paradigm dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a paradigm is established there are multiple competing schools, fact-gathering is relatively random, and researchers lack a common set of methods and phenomena to employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early stages feature natural histories and encyclopedic data that form a morass without implicit theoretical/methodological belief; different investigators may emphasize different subsets of phenomena, producing schools that later either vanish or are integrated into a paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of technology and crafts in early science
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology and established crafts (medicine, calendar making, metallurgy) are important sources of facts not casually discoverable and have often played a vital role in the emergence of new sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessible crafts yield recondite data that can seed scientific development; however, casual fact-collecting without theory can produce disorderly 'histories' that omit crucial details and hinder paradigm emergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of paradigm triumph and consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-paradigm school triumphs by emphasizing a tractable subset of phenomena and often producing new apparatus or results that others cannot ignore (e.g., Leyden jar and Franklin's synthesis), thereby providing a common paradigm for subsequent practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triumph is not total explanation of all facts but the ability to account for many effects and to direct future research productively; once a paradigm unites a group, research becomes more effective and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological consequences of paradigm adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a paradigm transforms the structure of the scientific group: older schools disappear or are marginalized, specialized journals and societies form, and the field acquires a more rigid definition that can exclude those unwilling or unable to accommodate to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who cling to older views may be read out of the profession or remain isolated; paradigm reception often signals formation of a profession or discipline with institutional markers (journals, societies, curriculum placement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift in research communication and readership
rubrics_metrics.description: With paradigms taken for granted, scientific communication shifts from books aimed at a broad educated audience to brief articles addressed to professional colleagues who share the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks abstract and encode the paradigm so creative scientists can begin research where textbooks leave off; the increasing esotericity of reports narrows intelligibility to non-specialists and is intrinsic to scientific advance rather than merely unfortunate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed research under a paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: A paradigm focuses research by indicating which problems are legitimate and which experiments are worth performing, enabling the design of specialized apparatus and sustained, precise investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigm-based research reduces random fact-gathering, concentrates effort on selected phenomena, and increases the efficiency and effectiveness of both fact collection and theory articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of methodological dichotomies
rubrics_metrics.description: Common dichotomies (e.g., 'context of discovery' vs 'context of justification', history vs logic) are problematic when applied to actual situations of knowledge gain, and may themselves be integral parts of traditional substantive answers that require historical observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distinctions are not prior logical/methodological premises but should be tested and recast based on how they function in real historical scientific practice; history of science provides phenomena to which theories about knowledge must apply.
